extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of social science, political economy, and methodology of the social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for conducting and evaluating sociological inquiry, contrasting the deductive (hypothetical) and inverse-deductive (historical) methods, and specifying how empirical laws, verification, and domain partitioning should be handled in social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit conditional assumptions in deductive models
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems of deductive science are hypothetical: grounded on some suppositious set of circumstances and declare how a given cause would operate in those circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the suppositions and limits clearly; conclusions are true only 'provided, and in as far as, the effect of those circumstances shall not be modified by others which have not been taken into the account.' To approach concrete truth include more individualizing circumstances, but note increasing complexity raises uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope of deductive inquiry to phenomena with few primary causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical combinations on which general theorems are constructed cannot be very complex without rapidly accumulating liability to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict deductive methods to classes of social facts that are principally influenced by a few causes; otherwise complexity deprives conclusions of value. Anti-pattern: applying geometrical-style deduction to phenomena dominated by many concurrent causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition social science into branches by primary causal class
rubrics_metrics.description: Different species of social facts are in the main dependent, immediately and in the first resort, on different kinds of causes; therefore they may and must be studied apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create distinct (though not independent) departments—e.g., Political Economy—for phenomena whose immediate determining causes are of one principal kind. Example: study industrial/distribution phenomena under the assumptions relevant to wealth-pursuit causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simplified behavioral assumptions for modelling (political-economy hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Economy considers mankind as occupied solely in acquiring and consuming wealth, making entire abstraction of every other human passion or motive except aversion to labor and desire of present enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the main acknowledged end as if sole for analytical convenience, then correct for other motives as needed. Note: this is a methodological device, not a literal claim about human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt theoretical conclusions to differing empirical premises
rubrics_metrics.description: When conclusions are drawn from premises adapted to one state of society, they require revision whenever applied to another whose elements differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace back demonstrations and introduce new premises in appropriate places before applying conclusions across societies. Example: English political-economy conclusions adapted to societies with different class/property structures (slave societies, state-landlord systems, small-holder contexts) must be revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect empirical laws from statistics and history for deductive use
rubrics_metrics.description: A preparatory treatment of observed facts—finding general propositions ('empirical laws')—fits them for collation with conclusions of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics and historical generalizations as necessary data for deductive science when direct observation of causes is impossible. Recognize these generalizations are approximate and may serve only as the best available inputs for theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify stability of remoter causes before generalizing empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws obtained indirectly (inferring causes from effects) can only be relied on so long as there is reason to think no change has taken place in any of the remote causes on which the immediate causes depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be well acquainted with remoter causes to avoid applying empirical laws to cases differing in those circumstances; failing to check them risks misapplication of statistical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain deductive oversight when using empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the best statistical generalizations must be constantly referred to the deductive science; the deductive science should stand sentinel over the whole process and sanction inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical data as inputs to be interpreted and validated by theory rather than as standalone proof; use theory to determine applicability and meaning of statistical regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of direct experimental verification in social cases
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a theory by an experiment, the circumstances must be exactly the same as those contemplated in the theory; in social phenomena the circumstances of no two cases are exactly alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect individual experiments or single-case trials to provide decisive verification; where direct verification is impossible, seek other modes (see indirect verification). Example: trial of corn laws in a different country would little verify theory about 'this generation and this country.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect verification across multiple cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Although direct verification is often impossible, conclusions are verified indirectly by the verification of other conclusions drawn in other individual cases from the same laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a theory by the degree it would have enabled us to predict what has actually occurred (retrodiction) and by its explanatory power across multiple instances rather than by single-case tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require retrodictive ability to validate predictive claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that our science renders us competent to predict the future, we must show that it would have enabled us to predict the present and the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the theory cannot account for existing facts, either search further among case-specific circumstances or extend/improve the theory. Use retrodiction as a key test of practical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account comprehensively for practical facts before cross-contextual application
rubrics_metrics.description: If we would apply our speculations (e.g., in political economy) to a country's phenomena, we must be able to explain all the mercantile or industrial facts of a general character and show causes sufficient to account for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to offer a comprehensive account indicates insufficient knowledge or imperfect theory, rendering one incompetent to draw practical or speculative conclusions for that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat historical uniformities as derivative and empirical, not natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of co-existence among social phenomena are corollaries from underlying causal laws and are empirical generalizations, not necessarily laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse observed historical patterns (e.g., sequences of societal states) with immutable natural laws; they require connection to psychological and ethological laws to attain scientific status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study laws of succession and co-existence among social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental problem of social science is to find the laws according to which any state of society produces the state which succeeds it and the uniformities of co-existence between the states of various social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'state of society' as the simultaneous state of many elements (knowledge, industry, beliefs, form of government, etc.) and seek causal laws of transition and co-existence among these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for progressiveness and historical change in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Social science deals with subject-matter whose properties change from age to age; reciprocal action of effects upon their causes produces progress or cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquire whether dynamics are trajectory (progress) or orbit (cycle); method must accommodate long-run change and generational replacement when theorizing and predicting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit compartmentalization where ethological differences are influential
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of social phenomena in which diversities of character between nations or times enter as influencing causes only in a secondary degree may be treated separately; phenomena mixed up with ethological influences cannot advantageously be treated independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating separate sciences (e.g., Science of Government) for topics inseparable from national character or other ethological causes; integrate ethological considerations where they are primary drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate political ethology when it has paramount influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of causes determining the type of character belonging to a people (Political Ethology) exercises a paramount influence over other branches and must be attended to for practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that national character heavily moulds customs, laws, government form, and subsequent social phenomena; neglecting ethology will vitiate practical applications of abstract branches like political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution inferring causation from specific experiences amid multiple interacting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the object is to determine the effect of any one social cause among many acting simultaneously, specific experience affords nothing amounting to empirical laws; the effect of one cause is disguised by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-interpreting averages from limited instances; exhaustive combinations of influential circumstances are unobtainable, and specific trials may not isolate single-cause effects (example: effects of corn laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address residual unexplained phenomena by seeking omitted circumstances or improving theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is any thing which we could not have predicted, this constitutes a residual phenomenon requiring further study to explain; we must either search among the circumstances of the particular case or extend and improve the theory itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat unexplained cases as prompts to either refine empirical knowledge of the case or to generalize the theoretical framework; neither option should be neglected when facing anomalies.
